paras: The lynching of Lloyd Clay took place in Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of May 14, 1919, when a mob of 800 to 1,000 took Clay, a young Black man, from the county jail, hanged and burned him and shot into his body. He was accused of attempted criminal assault on a young white woman who did not identify him. Black papers presented it as the burning of an innocent man, and the NAACP pressed Mississippi's governor to try the lynchers.

According to the wire account, a man entered the room of a young woman boarding at the home of Kelly Broussard early that morning and escaped after she screamed. Bloodhounds led officers to Clay at the Alabama and Vicksburg Railway station. The Vicksburg Evening Post, as reprinted by the Dallas Express, reported that Miss Hudson "declared he was not the man."

A crowd gathered at the jail and would not disperse, though Judge Brien offered a special grand jury if there was evidence. At 7:45 p.m. men battered a jail window with a length of railroad track, forced Sheriff Frank Scott to the floor, rammed a special deputy, M. G. Cockrell, and broke through three sets of steel doors to Clay's cell.

Clay protested his innocence; one wire version quoted him as beginning, "Give me a minute and I'll tell you who the other man," before he was cut off. He was driven by truck to an elm tree near the Broussard home, in front of Mrs. Ida M. Keefe's house. Oil was poured on his head, he was pulled up by the neck, his head was set alight with a fire beneath him, and shots were fired into the body. Stray bullets struck two white onlookers, Charles Lancaster, who was expected to die, and Bennie Stafford. The local account described women firing revolvers and a rush for pieces of rope as souvenirs when the body was cut down.

The Chicago Defender reported a coroner's verdict that Clay "met his death by mob violence, the said mob being unknown to the jury." No report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage; in June the New York Age said nothing had been done to punish the lynchers. Its correspondent added that 500 white citizens had signed a petition condemning the lynching. The NAACP telegraphed Governor Theodore G. Bilbo and Mayor J. J. Hayes on May 19, asking that the lynchers be brought to trial.
Black residents began leaving Vicksburg, and many burned the policies of a white insurance company whose collector was said to have been in the mob.

The Chicago Broad Ax and the Omaha Monitor first carried a short Associated Press dispatch on May 17 describing Clay as "alleged to have attacked a young white woman." A longer wire narrative ran in the St. Louis Argus and the Baltimore Afro-American on May 23 and in the Richmond Planet on June 7. It ended with the authorities' explanation that the lynching was "the culmination of feeling" over alleged attempts by Black men to attack white women.

The Defender headlined its correspondent's report "Fiends and Perverts Feed Lloyd Clay to Leaping Flames" and wrote that white residents called it "the most glorious celebration held in this city for many years." The New York Age ran "Innocent Man Is Lynched," and a Broad Ax editorial lamented that "an innocent man has been burned in that home of Jefferson Davis."

By contrast, white editorials reprinted in the Cleveland Advocate condemned the mob as an attack on the law while saying they had "no reason to doubt the guilt of the victim." In July the Dallas Express reprinted the Vicksburg papers' own coverage under the headline "The Burning of Lloyd Clay."

Accounts of the identification differ: the wire said the woman was not positive, the Evening Post that she said Clay was not the man, and the Defender that the crowd forced her to say "he is the man." The New York Age's correspondent reported a belief among Black residents that the intruder was a white man with whom she had been intimate. The Defender also wrote that the sheriff "stood idly by," contrary to the wire's account.

reader.title: Lynching of Lloyd Clay
bases: A mob took Clay from the Vicksburg jail, hanged, burned and shot him (A3, A4, A20).

A mob of 800 to 1,000 broke into the jail, overpowered the sheriff and killed Clay by hanging, burning and shooting (A1, A4, A20); it acted on an accusation of attempted criminal assault on a white girl, with no lawful authority (A4, A7).

The AP brief (A1), the longer wire narrative (A4, A20), the Defender's Vicksburg correspondent (A5), the Vicksburg papers' excerpts (A28, A30) and the New York Age's Jackson correspondent (A21) all report the jail break and the hanging and burning of Lloyd Clay.

accounts.label: Vicksburg Evening Post and Herald (reprinted)
accounts.gist: Miss Hudson declared Clay was not the man; the mob hanged and burned him before a crowd including women, who fired revolvers, and took rope as souvenirs.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Chicago Defender)
accounts.gist: Clay was innocent; Miss Hudson was forced by the crowd to say he was the man; the sheriff stood idly by; children took part; the coroner found the mob unknown.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (New York Age, Jackson)
accounts.gist: The intruder was reportedly a white man intimate with the woman; she said Clay was not the man and her father pleaded with the mob.

Defender headline 'Fiends and Perverts Feed Lloyd Clay to Leaping Flames' and 'Usual Verdict, Parties Unknown'; Afro-American 'Mississippi Crackers Hang And Burn Unidentified Prisoner'.
New York Age 'Innocent Man Is Lynched'; Broad Ax editorial on 'an innocent man' burned in 'that home of Jefferson Davis'.
Cleveland Advocate reprinted white editorials condemning the mob as an attack on law while stating 'no reason to doubt the guilt of the victim'.
